newsitem.title: UK: TREASURIES PARE LOSSES IN LONDON, EYE RETAIL DATA.
newsitem.headline: TREASURIES PARE LOSSES IN LONDON, EYE RETAIL DATA.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries rebounded from overnight lows in London on Wednesday, as attention focused on the upcoming U.S. retail sales data for any clues on robust growth in the third quarter.
"It's bouncing back a bit but I think if this retail sales figure is 0.7 percent or higher, it could begin to pull back even further," said one trader.
"We are trading very nervously, sentiment here is not positive," he added.
At 1015 GMT, the 30-year bond was quoted at 96-05 to yield 6.67 percent, from 95-28 in Tokyo and 96-05 in New York. The 10-year note was at 98-02 against 97-28 in Tokyo and 97-31 in New York.
In the futures market, September T-bonds slid below the previous day's low to 112-01, then pared it losses to stand 5/32 down on the day at 112-10 in automated trade.

The consensus expectation for July retail sales, due at 1230 GMT, is a rise of 0.7 percent in the headline figure from an 0.5 percent increase in June, and a rise of 0.5 percent ex-autos, from 0.3 percent.
But Adrian Schmidt, international economist at Chase in London, said he expected both the headline and ex-autos to rise by 0.4 percent.
"A figure of 0.7 would not be a big deal. The market is well aware that we're going to see a pickup in the third quarter," Schmidt said.

A strong figure would ignite an initial bout of selling "But I don't think it would be that dramatic. I would buy the initial move," he said, adding that retail sales tended to be volatile and large revisions were possible.
Also due at 1230 GMT are July producer prices, which according to a Reuters poll are expected to show a mild 0.1 percent rise after a 0.1 percent drop in the previous month.
But Schmidt said there was a danger of a higher number.
"If you see 0.7 retail sales and a PPI of 0.3 or something, forget it," said the London trader.
Most economists reckon U.S. growth will gather steam in the second half of the year after a summer lull, bringing the threat of higher inflation to the forefront.
But Schmidt said part of that growth could be absorbed by inventory accumulations. The GDP figure was unlikely to pick up to any great extent.
"It seems the Fed is not prepared to stick its neck out on this until there is some evidence that inflationary pressures are developing," he said.
